Where it began

John Campbell was born in Jamaica on 21 September 1993. He first caught the eye with the West Indies under-19s in Australia in 2012, where his 105 against England in the play-off for fifth place was the only hundred any West Indies batsman made at that World Cup.

He played his first senior match for Jamaica in the Caribbean Twenty20 of 2012–13 and moved into first-class and one-day cricket the season after. A maiden first-class hundred, 110 against the Leeward Islands, soon followed, and in 2015–16 his off-spin claimed seven for 73 against Trinidad and Tobago.

The player

His Test debut came against England in January 2019, and within two months he had played in all three formats for the West Indies against the same opponents. By November 2026 he had played 31 Tests, scoring 1,541 runs at 28.54 with one hundred, six fifties and a best of 115, and holding 20 catches.

The innings most people remember came in a one-day match against Ireland in 2019. Campbell made his first international hundred, and he and Shai Hope put on 365 for the first wicket, at the time the highest opening partnership in any one-day international. It was also the first time both openers in a one-day game had passed 150.

What made him special

Campbell was a left-hander who could score quickly once he was set. In one-day cricket openers are often asked only to see off the new ball, but on his good days he did a good deal more than that. Against India on 30 September 2026 he reached a one-day hundred in 65 balls, with nine fours and five sixes, then the fifth fastest by a West Indies batsman.

He bowled off-spin too, though by November 2026 his Test bowling had not brought him a wicket. That seven-wicket haul for Jamaica is a reminder to any captain that he is worth a try.

Away from the middle

He first played for Jamaica in January 2013 and soon became a regular in their side. He was named among the reserves for the 2019 World Cup and was picked in the Test squad for the 2020 series in England, which was put back to July.

And finally

Some batsmen spend a whole career waiting for their name to appear in the record books. Campbell got there on the same day as his first international hundred, and he had good company: Shai Hope at the other end, and 365 runs between them before anyone could part them.
